title: Inference and Margin of Error, Part 2: Medium and Hard Problems

beats.say: In part one, we scaled a sample proportion up to a population estimate, and we saw that an interval is the estimate plus or minus the margin of error.
In this video, we estimate a count and its complement, and then read two intervals from different towns to decide what can be concluded.

Medium example. A school has twenty-five hundred students. In a random sample of four hundred students, sixty said they prefer a morning start time. Estimate how many students at the school prefer a morning start, and how many do not.

card.sub: School: 2,500 students. Prefer, and do not prefer?

beats.say: Find the sample proportion, sixty out of four hundred, and multiply it by the number of students at the school.
Sixty divided by four hundred is zero point one five. So fifteen percent of the sample prefers a morning start.
Zero point one five times twenty-five hundred is three hundred seventy-five. So we estimate that about three hundred seventy-five students prefer a morning start.
To find how many students do not prefer a morning start, use the complement. Subtract the estimate from the total number of students.
Twenty-five hundred minus three hundred seventy-five is twenty-one hundred twenty-five. So about twenty-one hundred twenty-five students do not prefer it.

Hard example. In Town A, a random survey found plausible values for the percent owning an electric bike from forty-one point two to forty-six point eight. Town B's survey estimated forty-nine percent, with a margin of error of two points. What can be concluded?

card.sub: Town B: 49%, margin of error 2 points

beats.say: Town A's estimate is the midpoint of its interval, which is the average of the two endpoints.
Forty-one point two plus forty-six point eight is eighty-eight. We divide that by two.
Eighty-eight divided by two is forty-four. So Town A's estimate is forty-four percent.

scenes.title: Hard: Town A's margin of error

beats.say: The margin of error is half the width of the interval, so we subtract the lower endpoint from the upper one, and divide by two.
Forty-six point eight minus forty-one point two is five point six. We divide that by two.
Five point six divided by two is two point eight. So Town A's margin of error is two point eight percentage points.
Town B's interval is its estimate plus or minus its margin. Forty-nine minus two is forty-seven, and forty-nine plus two is fifty-one.
Now compare. Town A's interval tops out at forty-six point eight, and Town B's interval starts at forty-seven. The two intervals do not overlap.
Because the intervals do not overlap, there is convincing evidence that a greater percent of households in Town B own an electric bike.
If Town B's margin of error had been three points, its interval would start at forty-six, which overlaps Town A's interval. Then no clear conclusion could be drawn.
To recap. To estimate a count, multiply the sample proportion by the population. For the complement, subtract from the total.
beats.item: Estimate, then subtract for the complement

beats.say: From an interval, the estimate is the midpoint, and the margin of error is half the width.
Non-overlapping intervals give convincing evidence of a difference. In the next video, we look at common traps and the fast way.
